1009.title: The Green Revolution
1009.hook: Punjab's farms fed India, at a cost to water and soil
1009.howItsDone: Sikh families across Punjab farm, and gurdwaras and Sikh groups have joined farmers and scientists in campaigns about falling groundwater and the health of Punjab's soil.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Punjab reorganised, and your line was the language home. Did you speak a few words of a first language? Today, the new, smaller Punjab goes out into its fields. Day one thousand nine.

A sack of grain sits on a scale in a market yard, and a farmer in a turban watches the needle. Behind him, a tractor. Behind the tractor, a field of wheat so even it looks combed. Under the field, a pipe going down into the ground, pulling up water. Each of those things, the seed, the machine, the pipe, changed Punjab. The change got a big name: the Green Revolution. Its harvest fed a country. Its bill is still being paid in water and in soil.
screen: `GRAIN ON THE SCALE.` → `SEED, MACHINE, PIPE.` → `A HARVEST, AND A BILL.`

segments.voice: First, the seeds. New kinds of wheat, and then rice, gave far bigger harvests, as long as they had plenty of water and fertilizer. Punjab had rivers, canals and farmers ready to try them. Its grain went into the government's stores and out to the rest of India. That's today's line: fed a nation. Second, the farmer. At Ang 595 of the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Nanak borrows the farmer's year for the inner life: make the mind the plowman, good deeds the farming, effort the water and the body the field, and sow the Name as the seed. Tradition says Guru Nanak himself worked the fields in his later years. A Punjab farmer's whole day is already inside that hymn. Third, the cost. Rice is thirsty, and Punjab's own rains could not water it. Farmers sank tube wells deeper and deeper, and the water underground began to fall. Fertilizer and pesticide built up in the soil and the water. Some families took on debt for machines and seed. Farmers, scientists and Sikh groups have all raised the alarm, and not all of them agree on what should change. Fourth, the root. In the closing verse of Japji, at Ang 8, Guru Nanak calls air the guru, water the father, and the earth the great mother. Spoken beside a well that has to be dug deeper every few seasons, that line reads less like poetry and more like a plain description. In the hymn's terms, the water that fed a nation is a father, and the soil that carried the harvest is a mother. The Green Revolution is a story of a huge gift, and a question about how to thank the ones who gave it.
screen: `NEW SEEDS, BIG HARVESTS.` · `ANG 595: THE MIND AS PLOWMAN.` · `THE WATER FALLS, THE SOIL TIRES.` · `ANG 8: WATER THE FATHER, EARTH THE MOTHER.` · then, large: `FED A NATION.`

segments.voice: Start with your feet. If you can, put your feet flat on the floor, or your hand on a plant, or just picture a field. Think of the last thing you ate. Trace it back: the shop, the truck, the farmer, the field, the water under the field. Breathe in, and name one of them. Breathe out, and thank it. Keep going down the line, all the way to the soil. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each thank-you. The bell holds the time.
The Green Revolution. New seeds, water and machines that turned Punjab's fields into a granary for India, at a cost to its water and its soil. Today's word.
Your line: fed a nation. Today, before one meal, pause and name the field it came from, and leave nothing on the plate. Day one thousand nine.

1010.title: The Anandpur resolution, 1973
1010.hook: the Akali Dal set out demands for Punjab's rights, read very differently by different people
1010.howItsDone: The Anandpur Sahib resolution is still debated in Punjab politics; Akali leaders have described it as a call for federalism, and historians present its different readings and versions side by side.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Green Revolution, and your line was fed a nation. Did you name the field behind one meal? The fields were full, and the questions left open from the new map were still waiting. Day one thousand ten.

One document, two readers. The first reads it and sees a fair request: let a state run more of its own affairs. The second reads the very same pages and sees a warning sign: the start of breaking away. They may even be holding the same pages. What differs is the fear each brings to them. In the year in today's title, the Akali Dal met at Anandpur Sahib, the town where the Khalsa was born, and set down what it wanted for Punjab. That document is the Anandpur resolution, and how people read it shaped the years that followed.
screen: `ONE DOCUMENT, TWO READERS.` → `A FAIR ASK, OR A WARNING?` → `MET AT ANANDPUR SAHIB.`

segments.voice: First, the place. Anandpur Sahib is where tradition says Guru Gobind Singh called the Khalsa into being. Meeting there tied the demands to the heart of the panth's story. Second, what it asked. Histories summarize it like this. The central government should keep a short list of powers, such as defense, foreign affairs and currency, and leave the rest to the states. Chandigarh should go to Punjab. Punjab's share of the river waters should be settled fairly. And it set out religious and social aims for the Sikhs as well. Third, the two readings. Akali leaders said it was about federalism: more say for every state, not just Punjab, inside India. Critics in Delhi and elsewhere read it as a step toward a separate Sikh country. It didn't help that more than one version of the text went around, and people quoted the version that fit their fear. Historians still describe it in different ways. Fourth, the root. At Ang 97 of the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Arjan says that all are partners in the Lord's care, and no one is outside it. A partner's voice is worth hearing in full, before it's labeled. When one text is read two ways, the work is to find out what each reader is afraid of. That's today's line: read both sides.
screen: `ANANDPUR: WHERE THE KHALSA BEGAN.` · `FEWER POWERS FOR THE CENTER.` · `FEDERALISM, OR BREAKING AWAY?` · `ANG 97: ALL ARE PARTNERS.` · then, large: `READ BOTH SIDES.`

segments.voice: Two minutes to read both sides of one issue. Sit upright, and let the breath even out. Choose one argument in your life or in the news where you already know whose side you're on. Breathe in, and say to yourself, as fairly as you can, what your side wants. Breathe out, and say what the other side wants, in words they would recognize. Breathe in, and name what your side fears. Breathe out, and name what theirs fears. You don't have to change your mind. Just hear both. If you pray, you can rest on Waheguru at the end. The bell holds the time.
The Anandpur resolution. The Akali Dal's statement of what it wanted for Punjab, read by some as a plea for fair federalism and by others as a step toward breaking away. Today's word.
Your line: read both sides. Today, before you share an opinion on something that divides people, read one honest piece from the side you disagree with. Day one thousand ten.

1011.title: Amritsar, 1978
1011.hook: a clash between Sikhs and the Sant Nirankari sect left people dead and tensions rising
1011.howItsDone: Some histories of Punjab treat the Vaisakhi clash in Amritsar as a turning point toward the conflict that followed; those killed among the protesters are remembered in some Sikh circles as martyrs.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Anandpur resolution, and your line was read both sides. Did you read one honest piece from the other side? Today, two groups in one city, and a day that went wrong. Day one thousand eleven.

Vaisakhi, the spring festival, the day Sikhs remember the birth of the Khalsa. Amritsar is full of pilgrims. And across the city, a different group is holding its own gathering: the Sant Nirankaris, followers of a living guru. To some Sikhs, holding that gathering in the Guru's own city, on that day, is an insult. A group of Sikhs sets out to protest. By evening, people are dead, and the city is not the same. Today's word is the city itself: Amritsar.
screen: `VAISAKHI IN AMRITSAR.` → `TWO GATHERINGS, ONE CITY.` → `BY EVENING, PEOPLE ARE DEAD.`

segments.voice: First, the quarrel. Sikhs hold that the line of human Gurus ended with Guru Gobind Singh, and that the Guru now lives in the Guru Granth Sahib and in the Khalsa panth. The Sant Nirankaris followed a living guru of their own, and some Sikhs heard things said in their gatherings as mocking the Sikh Gurus. The Nirankaris saw themselves as a spiritual movement free to teach as they chose. Second, the day. Sikhs from the Akhand Kirtani Jatha, and followers of Jarnail Singh Bhindranwale, head of the Damdami Taksal, marched toward the Nirankari gathering to protest. Shots were fired. Sikh protesters were killed, and so were some Nirankaris. Accounts still differ about who struck first. Third, what followed. Courts, edicts and anger. The Akal Takht issued a hukamnama telling Sikhs to keep away from the Nirankaris. Bhindranwale's voice grew louder, and violence between the two groups went on. That's today's line: tension rose. Fourth, the root. Among Sheikh Farid's verses in the Guru Granth Sahib, at Ang 1382, is a short one: do good even to the one who does you wrong, and don't let anger settle in your mind. That line had stood in the Guru Granth Sahib for centuries before that Vaisakhi. The story of these years is partly the story of how hard that line is to live when people feel their Guru has been insulted. Remembering the day honestly means holding the grief of every family who lost someone in it.
screen: `A LIVING GURU, AND THE GURU GRANTH.` · `A PROTEST, THEN SHOTS.` · `A HUKAMNAMA, AND LOUDER VOICES.` · `ANG 1382: DON'T LET ANGER SETTLE.` · then, large: `TENSION ROSE.`

segments.voice: Two minutes for peace between groups. Sit, and rest your hands. Bring to mind two groups you know of who don't trust each other: in your town, your family, your country, anywhere. Don't decide who's right. Breathe in, and see one ordinary person from the first group, at their own kitchen table. Breathe out, and see one from the second, at theirs. Then hold both tables at once, and wish both of them a quiet evening. If you pray, you can pray for peace between them in your own words, or rest on Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Amritsar. The Guru's city, where a Vaisakhi protest against the Sant Nirankaris ended in killing, and tension rose across Punjab. Today's word.
Your line: tension rose. Today, when you feel tension rising in a room, be the one who lowers your voice instead of raising it. Day one thousand eleven.

1012.title: June 1984, remembered again
1012.hook: in Sikh remembrance, the June 1984 attack is the third ghallughara
1012.howItsDone: Sikhs remember the June attack on the Darbar Sahib each year, with gatherings at the Akal Takht and in gurdwaras, where those who died are remembered in prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Amritsar, and your line was tension rose. When tension rose around you, did you lower your voice? Today the tension in that city breaks, and this path comes back to a June it has met before. Day one thousand twelve.

Some words are names for a single thing. Others are names for a kind of thing, so that when something new happens, people reach for the old word and add a number. Sikhs have such a word. It belongs to the long story this year has been walking: two great massacres of Sikhs, long ago, remembered as the small and the great ghallughara. When the army entered the Darbar Sahib in the June this lesson is named for, a new event got the old word. In Sikh remembrance it is the third ghallughara.
screen: `AN OLD WORD, A NEW NUMBER.` → `THE SMALL AND THE GREAT.` → `THE THIRD GHALLUGHARA.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Ghallughara means a holocaust, a massacre, a great destruction. This path met the small ghallughara and the great ghallughara earlier this year, in the years when Sikhs were hunted and killed. Second, the June. The government called it Operation Blue Star. Bhindranwale and armed followers had fortified the Darbar Sahib complex, and the army was sent in to remove them. It came during the days Sikhs gather to remember the martyrdom of Guru Arjan, the Guru who compiled the Adi Granth, so the complex was full of pilgrims. Pilgrims died alongside fighters and soldiers. The Akal Takht was badly damaged in the fighting. The Sikh Reference Library, with its old handwritten books, burned. Third, the naming. Calling June the third ghallughara puts it in a line with the two earlier massacres. It says this belongs to the Sikh story of suffering, and is remembered the same way: in gatherings and in prayer, every June. Others, including the government of the day, described it as a military operation against armed militants. Both descriptions are part of the record. Fourth, the root. Guru Arjan, whose martyrdom the pilgrims had come to mark, wrote at Ang 394 that whatever the Lord does seems sweet to him. Sikhs remember that line beside his martyrdom. Holding it in June is not saying that what happened was sweet. It is how a tradition grieves without letting go of its Guru. That's today's line: the third ghallughara.
screen: `GHALLUGHARA: A GREAT DESTRUCTION.` · `PILGRIMS INSIDE, FOR GURU ARJAN.` · `A LINE WITH THE EARLIER TWO.` · `ANG 394: YOUR WILL SEEMS SWEET.` · then, large: `THE THIRD GHALLUGHARA.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with a lamp for the pilgrims. If you can, light a candle or a small lamp; if not, picture one. Sit, and look at the flame. The pilgrims came that June to remember a Guru's martyrdom, and some never went home. Breathe in, and let the light stand for them, the old and the young, without names. Breathe out, and hold their families. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. Then let the flame burn. The bell holds the time.
Ghallughara. A great destruction, a massacre. Sikh memory holds two from the long story, and calls the June attack on the Darbar Sahib the third. Today's word.
Your line: the third ghallughara. Today, find one name, or one face, of someone lost in a grief that isn't yours, and remember it quietly. Day one thousand twelve.

1013.title: The widows' colony
1013.hook: widows of November 1984 were resettled in one Delhi colony and raised children alone
1013.howItsDone: Sikhs remember the November killings each year in gurdwaras and at gatherings in Delhi, and Sikh groups have supported the widows and children of Tilak Vihar with schooling, work and help through the courts.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ghallughara, and your line was the third ghallughara. Whose name did you hold for a moment? Today the story moves from June to November, and from Amritsar to Delhi. Day one thousand thirteen.

A school uniform hangs on a nail. A mother irons it before dawn, packs a lunch, walks a child to the bus stop, and then goes to work. Plenty of households run on mornings like that. In one neighborhood in West Delhi, street after street of those mornings were run by women alone, because their husbands, brothers and grown sons had been killed in a few days in November. The government gave them flats there. People began calling the place by a name that stuck: the widows' colony.
screen: `A UNIFORM, A LUNCH, A BUS STOP.` → `MOTHERS ALONE, STREET AFTER STREET.` → `THE WIDOWS' COLONY.`

segments.voice: First, the November. After Prime Minister Indira Gandhi was shot by two of her Sikh bodyguards, mobs went through Delhi and other cities hunting Sikh men. Homes were burned. Men were beaten and burned in front of their families. Survivors and later inquiries said the police often stood by, and some officials and politicians were accused of leading the mobs. Second, the colony. Widows and their children from neighborhoods the mobs had struck were given flats in Tilak Vihar, in West Delhi. Women who had never earned a wage took jobs, often humble ones, to keep children fed and in school. That's today's line: they raised them alone. Third, the long after. Some children grew up angry and without work; some fell into drugs; others studied hard and climbed out. The mothers went to court, again and again, to testify. Justice moved slowly, and for some families it still feels unfinished. Fourth, the root. In Asa di Var, at Ang 473, Guru Nanak asks why anyone would call woman lesser, when from her kings are born. The women of the colony were not given a choice about becoming the head of a household. But they carried it, and the gurbani they heard in their gurdwara had already said they were never lesser. The colony's real story isn't the days of the killing. It's the long run of ordinary mornings after it.
screen: `NOVEMBER: THE MOBS.` · `FLATS IN TILAK VIHAR.` · `CHILDREN, COURTS, THE LONG AFTER.` · `ANG 473: FROM HER, KINGS ARE BORN.` · then, large: `THEY RAISED THEM ALONE.`

segments.voice: Someone is raising a child mostly alone tonight. Sit, and let the breath slow down by itself. Bring one such person to mind: a neighbor, a coworker, a cousin, your own parent once. Breathe in, and picture one of their ordinary mornings: the alarm, the lunch, the rush. Breathe out, and wish them strength for it. Then think of one small, real help you could give this week. A meal, a school pickup, a message. If you pray, you can hold them in Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
The widows' colony. The name people gave to Tilak Vihar in West Delhi, where widows of November were resettled and raised their children alone. Today's word.
Your line: they raised them alone. Today, do one practical thing for someone raising a child on their own, and don't wait to be asked. Day one thousand thirteen.

1014.title: The Punjab years
1014.hook: violence by militants and by police killed people across Punjab; a human-rights worker, Jaswant Singh Khalra, documented disappearances and was killed
1014.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Jaswant Singh Khalra as a defender of human rights; families of the disappeared and human rights groups continue to seek records and justice for those killed in these years.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the widows' colony, and your line was they raised them alone. Did you do one practical thing for someone raising a child? Today the story goes back to Punjab, into the hardest years. Day one thousand fourteen.

A ledger in a city office: dates, firewood, and a line that says unidentified. Then another line, and another. The cremation ground keeps records of the wood it buys to burn the dead. A man from Amritsar named Jaswant Singh Khalra asked to see those records. He began adding up the lines marked unidentified, and he began asking a simple, dangerous question: who were they? Today, the years when Punjab burned from more than one side, and the man who counted the missing.
screen: `A LEDGER: FIREWOOD, UNIDENTIFIED.` → `WHO WERE THEY?` → `THE MAN WHO COUNTED.`

segments.voice: First, the violence from one side. After the June and the November, armed militants fighting for a separate Sikh state called Khalistan killed police and officials, and they also killed ordinary people: Hindus, and Sikhs who disagreed with them. Buses were stopped. Markets were bombed. Second, the violence from the other. Police fighting the militants were given wide powers, and young Sikh men were picked up, tortured, killed in staged encounters, or simply disappeared. Families went to police stations and were told their sons had never been there. Both of these are part of the record, and Punjab's families carry both. Third, the counting. Jaswant Singh Khalra worked for the human rights wing of the Akali Dal. He went through cremation ground records in Amritsar district and found bodies cremated as unidentified, lines he believed were the disappeared. He published what he found and spoke about it, in India and abroad. Then he himself was taken from outside his home and killed. Police officers were later convicted for his abduction and murder. That's today's line: he counted the missing. Fourth, the root. In the hymns Guru Nanak sang about the violence of Babur's armies, at Ang 723, he says that he speaks the word of truth, and will tell the truth at the time for truth. Khalra did not pick up a weapon. He picked up a ledger. He is remembered for that.
screen: `MILITANTS KILLED POLICE AND CIVILIANS.` · `POLICE TORTURE AND DISAPPEARANCES.` · `KHALRA OPENED THE LEDGERS.` · `ANG 723: TRUTH AT THE TIME FOR TRUTH.` · then, large: `HE COUNTED THE MISSING.`

segments.voice: Two minutes to honor someone who told the truth. Sit still for a moment, and breathe. Bring to mind one person who told a hard truth when it cost them: a whistleblower, a journalist, a friend who said what no one else would, maybe someone in your own family. Breathe in, and see their face. Breathe out, and thank them, silently. Then ask yourself what one small truth you have been keeping quiet. You don't have to act on it now. Just hold it. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
The Punjab years. The time after the June and the November, when militants and police both killed, and Jaswant Singh Khalra counted the disappeared. Today's word.
Your line: he counted the missing. Today, read or share the true story of one person who was disappeared or silenced somewhere, so their name is counted once more. Day one thousand fourteen.

1015.title: Peace returns
1015.hook: Punjab grew quieter, and families began to heal
1015.howItsDone: Sikh families who lost loved ones in these years remember them in Ardas and in gurdwara programs, and some still seek records and justice while getting on with daily life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Punjab years, and your line was he counted the missing. Did you read one true story of someone silenced? Today, at the end of a hard week, the guns go quiet. Day one thousand fifteen.

A shopkeeper in a Punjab town pulls his shutter down long after dark, for the first time in years. Nobody knocks. Nothing happens. He walks home. That's what peace looked like in Punjab when it came back: not a parade, but small, ordinary things done again without fear. A farmer turning water onto his field at night. A wedding with music until late. Buses running on time. Slowly, the fighting faded, and Punjab grew quieter. Today is about what comes after the quiet.
screen: `A SHUTTER DOWN AFTER DARK.` → `A FIELD WATERED AT NIGHT.` → `WHAT COMES AFTER THE QUIET.`

segments.voice: First, the quiet. The armed groups were broken up or faded away, elections were held again, and ordinary life came back to towns and villages. Historians argue about how it happened and at what cost, and about how much of it came from police force. Less disputed is that daily life changed. Second, what the quiet didn't fix. Mothers were still waiting for sons who had disappeared. Widows in Delhi were still going to court. Families on every side had empty chairs at the table. Peace stopped new wounds. It did not close the old ones. That's today's line: healing, slowly. Third, the medicine. In Asa di Var, at Ang 469, Guru Nanak says something strange: suffering became the medicine, and comfort the disease. Pain, in that line, can push a person back toward the Lord, where easy days let them forget. Some Sikh families who lived through these years turned to gurbani, to sangat and to seva, not to erase what happened, but to carry it. Fourth, a look back. This week began in Punjab's green fields. Then came the Anandpur resolution, read two ways; a Vaisakhi clash in Amritsar; June, remembered as the third ghallughara; the widows' colony in Delhi; and Khalra counting the missing. It ends here, with quiet, and the slow work after it. Healing is not forgetting. It is learning to live beside the empty chair.
screen: `THE GUNS GO QUIET.` · `PEACE DID NOT CLOSE OLD WOUNDS.` · `ANG 469: SUFFERING, THE MEDICINE.` · `A WEEK FROM FIELDS TO QUIET.` · then, large: `HEALING, SLOWLY.`

segments.voice: Sit, and slow the breath a little. Bring to mind one wound that hasn't closed: your own, or a family's, or a place's. Don't try to fix it. Breathe in, and let it be there. Breathe out, and let the breath be a little longer than the breath in. Healing doesn't happen in two minutes, and it doesn't need to. You're just sitting beside it. If you pray, you can pray for healing in your own words, or rest on Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Peace returns. The time when the fighting faded and Punjab grew quieter, and families began the slow work of healing. Today's word.
Your line: healing, slowly. Today, be patient with one wound, yours or someone else's, and don't ask it to heal faster than it can. Day one thousand fifteen.
